about-these-standards.title: About these Standards
about-these-standards.markdown:
The SFEDI Business Support Standards set out what good business support looks like: what a professional supporting businesses needs to be able to do, and what they need to know and understand to do it well.

They are the evolution of the national standards for business support that SFEDI first developed and published between 2007 and 2010: the Business Support, Business Information and Introduction to Enterprise Support standards. SFEDI's standards were updated in 2013 as the national Business and Enterprise Support standards. Together, they have underpinned qualifications, recruitment, appraisal, CPD and the contracting of business support for nearly two decades. This edition keeps what has stood the test of practice, removes duplication and dated references, and adds what business support professionals now need, including AI and digital adoption, sustainability, data protection, today's finance landscape, working with neurodivergent and disabled clients, and evidencing impact.

References to business throughout should be taken to mean all kinds and forms of enterprise, including self-employment, sole traders, family businesses, social enterprises and co-operatives.

who-they-are-for.title: Who they are for
who-they-are-for.markdown:
- Business advisers, mentors, coaches, consultants and trainers who support people starting, running and growing businesses
- Professionals who serve small businesses, such as accountants, bookkeepers, solicitors and bank staff
- People who design, commission and manage business support programmes
- Training and CPD providers who want to align their programmes to a recognised benchmark
- Employers who recruit, develop and appraise business support staff

how-the-standards-are-structured.title: How the Standards are structured
how-the-standards-are-structured.markdown:
| Part | What it covers |
|---|---|
| Professional behaviours (B1 to B11) | The behaviours expected in every area of business support. They apply to every Standard |
| Core Standards (C1 to C8) | The main functions of a business support professional, which every practitioner is expected to meet |
| Specialist Standards (S1 to S27) | Areas of specialist practice that build on the Core Standards |
| Business Information Standards (I1 to I4) | Information, enquiry and front-line roles, such as helplines, enquiry teams and first-point-of-contact navigators |
| Introduction to Business Support Standards (E1 to E5) | For people thinking of working in business support or new to it, as a basis for progressing to the Core Standards |

how-to-read-a-standard.title: How to read a Standard
how-to-read-a-standard.markdown:
Each Standard follows the format used in the original SFEDI standards:

- **Summary**: what the Standard is about and who it applies to
- **What you need to show**: the performance requirements your practice must meet, coded (for example C1.1)
- **What you need to know and understand**: the knowledge that underpins that practice, coded (for example C1.K1)
- **Evolved from**: the original SFEDI standards it replaces or draws on

Specialist Standards also say who they are for. Codes start with C for Core, S for Specialist, I for Business Information and E for Introduction (entry).

how-the-standards-are-used.title: How the Standards are used
how-the-standards-are-used.markdown:
**By professionals**, to assess their own practice, plan CPD and show clients and employers what they can do.

**By employers and commissioners**, to write job descriptions, recruit and develop staff, and specify the quality of support they expect from providers.

standards-in-specialist-certification.title: Specialist Certification and the Standards
standards-in-specialist-certification.markdown: **Through Specialist Certification.** Professionals can be certified against a Specialist Standard through SFEDI Specialist Programmes, CPD or workshops.

standards-in-specialist-programmes.title: SFEDI Specialist Programmes and the Standards
standards-in-specialist-programmes.markdown: **Through SFEDI Specialist Programmes.** Training and CPD providers can map their workshops and programmes to the Specialist Standards and apply to SFEDI for approval. SFEDI then certificates learners who complete them.

mapping-a-programme-to-the-standards.title: Mapping a programme to the Standards
mapping-a-programme-to-the-standards.markdown:
Every requirement has its own code so that programmes and evidence can be mapped precisely.

- Performance requirements (for example S3.4) describe what a professional does in practice. Evidence for these must come from real client work, or from realistic practice where SFEDI agrees.
- Knowledge requirements (for example S3.K2) can be evidenced through learning and assessment, such as assignments, questions, case studies or professional discussion.
- A SFEDI Specialist Programme states which codes it covers, how it covers them and how learning is checked.
- Professional behaviours are demonstrated through practice and are assumed in every Standard.

framework.coreIntro: The Core Standards describe the main functions of a business support professional. Every practitioner working to these Standards is expected to meet them, whatever their role or specialism.
framework.specialistIntro: The Specialist Standards describe areas of specialist practice. They build on the Core Standards, which are assumed throughout. Each Specialist Standard has one matching SFEDI Specialist Certification.
framework.informationIntro: The Business Information Standards describe information, enquiry and front-line roles in business support, such as helplines, enquiry teams and the navigators who are the first point of contact for business support services. People in these roles also work to C7 (Practise ethically and professionally), C8 (Develop own practice and networks) and the professional behaviours, with business knowledge at the level set out in E5. The numbering follows the original Business Information Standards.
framework.introductionIntro: The Introduction to Business Support Standards are for people who are thinking of working in business support, or who are new to it. They help people identify whether they have the abilities, knowledge and experience that provide a basis for developing into a business support role, such as business adviser or mentor. They can be used for self-assessment, introductory and taster programmes, and entry-level learning. The phrase "the people you are working with" can apply to colleagues as well as clients. The numbering follows the original Introduction to Enterprise Support standards.
framework.behavioursIntro: Every professional working to these Standards is expected to show the following behaviours. They apply to every Core and Specialist Standard, so they are not repeated in each one.

behaviours.text: Put the client's interests first and act with honesty, integrity and impartiality
Be open with clients about what you can offer, keep your commitments to them and protect their confidentiality
Shape your approach around each client's goals, circumstances and ways of working, and show empathy with clients from all walks of life
Listen carefully, ask searching but even-handed questions, confirm you have understood, and speak and write clearly and simply
Build trust across the whole of a working relationship, and encourage open, two-way feedback
Look at the whole picture, gather the information you need, reach well-founded conclusions and offer options you can justify
Use what you know and have experienced, while staying curious about new ideas, evidence and technology
Deal with disagreement, resistance, setbacks and uncertainty calmly and constructively
Know the limits of your competence, and seek or refer to specialist help when a situation goes beyond them
Treat every client fairly and work inclusively with people from all backgrounds and circumstances
Keep learning and developing so that your practice keeps improving

standards.title: Build and manage professional client relationships
standards.evolvedFrom: Business Support 1 (Maintain effective business support relationships with clients); Business Information 1 (in part); Introduction to Enterprise Support 1; Business and Enterprise Support (2013) units 1, 3 and 4.
standards.summary: This is about establishing, managing and ending professional relationships with clients, whether you are working with an individual or a team, so that they trust you and the service you represent. It covers agreeing what support will be provided, communicating in the ways that suit each client, building credibility, handling difficulties, keeping accurate records and closing each engagement well. It also covers reaching people who could benefit from support and explaining clearly what you offer.

performanceRequirements.text: Agree with the client what support you will provide, who is responsible for what, any costs, and what any contract or funding conditions do and do not allow
Keep in touch with each client through the channels that suit them, including face to face, telephone, video and digital channels
Create conversations in which the client, or each member of a client team, feels able to talk openly about the business and the personal matters that affect it
When working with a client team or a family business, establish who does what, what each person needs and how much influence they have
Help the client put into words what they want to achieve, for the business and for themselves
Notice when a client is anxious, under pressure or struggling, talk to them about it with care, and direct them to appropriate personal or specialist support
Build credibility and trust with clients and relevant stakeholders through consistent and reliable delivery
Give constructive feedback, encourage the client to give feedback, and use it to strengthen the relationship
Recognise and manage disagreement or conflict with clients constructively, involving others where this would help
Record client contact, agreed actions and outcomes accurately, promptly and securely, in line with data protection requirements
Check with the client at regular points how well the relationship and the support are working for them, and adjust where needed
Close each engagement in a planned way, agreeing next steps and leaving the door open for the client to come back
Explain clearly to potential clients what support you offer, how it could help them and any costs, in person and online
Reach and engage potential clients through networks, referral partners and other channels, including people less likely to seek support

knowledgeRequirements.text: The interpersonal and communication skills that support effective client work, including active listening, open and probing questions, summarising and reflecting, constructive challenge, negotiation, feedback and handling difficult conversations
When each way of communicating works best (for example face to face, telephone, video, email, messaging and online platforms), and how to make each accessible
How to adapt your communication for people of different backgrounds, cultures and communication needs, including neurodivergent people, and how to make reasonable adjustments
How to contract a support relationship, covering scope, roles, boundaries, costs, timescales and how it will end
How the personality, competence, role and level of authority of the people you work with can affect a support relationship, and how to work with them
The eligibility conditions and contractual obligations of the services you deliver, including those attached to public funding
The signs that a client may need personal support (for example with wellbeing, mental health or personal debt), and where to direct them
Your organisation's requirements for recording client information, and the data protection rules that apply to client records
How to prevent, manage and resolve conflict in a support relationship
How to develop and communicate a clear value proposition for the support you provide
Approaches to reaching and engaging potential clients, including under-represented groups, and how to judge which work

standards.title: Diagnose needs and analyse the business
standards.evolvedFrom: Business Support 2 (Help the client to analyse the business and decide the way forward); Business Information 1 and 2 (in part); Business and Enterprise Support (2013) units 2, 5 and 8.
standards.summary: This is about helping clients to build a clear, evidence-based picture of their business: where it is, where it is heading and what needs to change. It involves gathering and analysing information, using recognised diagnostic tools, separating the symptoms of problems from their causes and agreeing priorities. Wherever possible you should work in a way that helps clients develop these analytical skills for themselves.

performanceRequirements.text: Invite the client to share their own view of how the business is performing, where it is heading and what matters to them and its stakeholders
Gather and structure information about the client's business, its market and its operating environment, using appropriate questioning, data and research
Use recognised measures and diagnostic tools with the client to build a shared understanding of where the business stands now
Distinguish between the symptoms and the root causes of business problems
Help the client pinpoint the opportunities open to the business and what is holding its performance back
Help the client weigh up possible changes in terms of their objectives, the risks and benefits, and the resources they can draw on
Encourage the client to set objectives for the short, medium and longer term that are realistic, precise and stretching, for themselves and the business
Develop clear, evidence-based recommendations that support the client's decision making
Agree with the client the priorities and the way forward, and help them record it in a form of plan suited to the business
Help the client involve other stakeholders and build their support for the way forward
Build the client's own ability to analyse their business, so they rely less on outside help over time

knowledgeRequirements.text: Qualitative and quantitative diagnostic techniques (for example SWOT, PESTLE, five forces, business model and value proposition analysis, benchmarking and maturity assessments)
Key performance indicators and other measures of business performance, and how to read them
How to find and use reliable sources of business and market information, including official statistics and online data, and how to judge their quality
Problem definition and root cause analysis techniques
Techniques for identifying and assessing business risk

The typical challenges and opportunities for businesses of different sizes and stages, and in different business models (including social enterprises, family businesses, franchising, licensing and distribution agreements)
How to spot trends and developments likely to affect the client's business (for example customer demand, new technology including AI, regulation, energy and climate, and international trade)
How to set objectives, and how to structure a business or growth plan that suits the size and needs of the business
How to map stakeholders and their influence, and how to win their backing
How to understand a business's culture and what drives, enables and limits the people in it
How social, cultural and religious values can shape the way people run their businesses

standards.title: Support action and change
standards.evolvedFrom: Business Support 3 (Enable clients to implement changes in their business); Business Support 4 (Encourage clients to act for themselves); Business Support 15 (in part); Introduction to Enterprise Support 4; Business and Enterprise Support (2013) units 8, 9, 10 and 16 (in part).
standards.summary: This is about helping clients turn decisions into action, sustain change and become more capable, confident and independent. It involves action planning, supporting implementation and adapting when circumstances change. It also involves choosing the mode of support that suits the client and the stage of the relationship, whether that is advising, mentoring, coaching, facilitating, training or consultancy.

performanceRequirements.text: Gauge how ready the client is to make changes, and help them build the commitment to follow through
Draw out the client's doubts about change, including those they have not voiced, and address them with evidence and reasoning
Develop an action plan with the client covering what they want to achieve, the steps, who does what and by when, the resources needed, the risks and how progress will be tracked
Be clear with the client about your part in supporting the plan, and what other support or resources they will need
Select the type of support that best fits the client and the point you have reached together (for example advising, mentoring or coaching), and tell the client when you switch between them
Find out how the client learns best, and work in those ways
Support the client as they put the plan into action and track it, adapting it when circumstances change or things do not go to plan
Help the client work through personal or relationship issues that could block change
Work with the client in ways that build their skills, knowledge, confidence and independence
Sustain the client's momentum by giving feedback and recognising the progress they make

knowledgeRequirements.text: The signs of a client's readiness and commitment to change, and the factors behind them (for example ambivalence, competing priorities and long-standing habits)
Techniques for planning actions, setting priorities, preparing for contingencies and comparing risks with benefits
How advising, mentoring, coaching, facilitation, training and consultancy differ, and when each is the right choice
Styles of consulting intervention (for example acceptant, catalytic, confrontational and prescriptive) and their effects
How adults learn (for example the experiential learning cycle), and how to adapt your approach to different learning preferences and needs
How self-doubt, limiting beliefs, weak routines or personal circumstances can hold a client back, and how to help

How a client's circumstances, including disability, neurodiversity, gender, ethnicity, age, sexual orientation, caring responsibilities and reliance on benefits, can shape their experience of running a business, and the support available
How to support decisions without taking them over, so that the client stays in control
How to involve and delegate to others in delivering an action plan

standards.title: Navigate, refer and broker support
standards.evolvedFrom: Business Support 10 (Broker clients to business support services); Business Support 13 (Help the client to critically assess a business support service provider's offer); Business Support 14 (Broker deals with business support service providers); Business Support 15 (Help the client to build confidence and capacity to evaluate and broker their own solutions); Business Support 5 (in part); Business and Enterprise Support (2013) units 4 (in part), 14, 15 and 16. C4 covers finding, explaining and referring to support; S25 (Brokering Specialist Support) covers helping clients specify, select, fund and manage providers in depth.
standards.summary: This is about helping clients, impartially, to find, access and evaluate the support they need from others. It involves knowing the national, local and sector support available, explaining the options, referring clients well and following up, while making sure the client keeps responsibility for their own decisions. Over time it means building the client's ability to do this for themselves.

performanceRequirements.text: Identify the national, local and sector support relevant to the client's needs, including public programmes, finance, specialist advice and peer networks
Explain the options available to the client, including costs, eligibility and any public subsidy involved
Refer or introduce the client to appropriate services, explaining why, and with the client's consent to share their information
Stay impartial throughout, leaving the choice of provider, and how to use them, with the client
Follow up referrals to check they have met the client's needs, and act on problems within your responsibility
Help the client become confident and capable of finding and judging support for themselves in future
Use feedback from clients and colleagues on providers to improve the quality of future referrals

knowledgeRequirements.text: The current landscape of business support, including national services, local and regional provision, and sector, private and voluntary provision, and how to keep up to date with it
The sources of finance and funding available for business support and business development
Referral procedures and eligibility rules, and how to obtain and record consent to share client information
How to judge whether a referral or another provider's support has met the client's needs
The records to keep of referrals

standards.title: Measure and evidence impact
standards.evolvedFrom: Business Support 8 (Monitor the performance of the business support service); Business Support 15 (items f to h); Business Support 17 (item h); Business Support 6 (in part); Business and Enterprise Support (2013) units 12 and 16 (in part).
standards.summary: This is about agreeing with clients how success will be judged, reviewing progress and outcomes, and recording and reporting evidence of impact for clients, your organisation, commissioners and funders. It also covers using what you learn to improve the support provided, by you and by your organisation.

performanceRequirements.text: Agree with the client at the start what success will look like, and when and how you will review progress together
Help the client identify indicators and methods for measuring the impact of the support on their business
At the agreed points, look back with the client at progress against their objectives and plan
Help the client assess the effect of the support on the business, distinguishing it from other influences
Invite the client to tell you about any problems with the support, look into them, and put them right yourself or pass them to whoever can
Record outcomes and impact accurately and consistently, in line with organisational, contractual and data protection requirements
Report evidence of impact clearly to those who need it, including clients, your organisation, commissioners and funders
Report where support may breach legislation, regulations, contractual terms or organisational guidelines
Use findings and feedback to recommend and make improvements to the support provided by you and your organisation

knowledgeRequirements.text: Why monitoring and evaluation matter to clients, organisations, commissioners and funders
Measures of business outcomes and impact (for example turnover, profit, productivity, jobs, investment, survival, skills and environmental performance) and their limitations
Methods of collecting evidence of impact, including client feedback, case studies, before-and-after measures and follow-up
The principles of attribution and additionality, and the limits of what can reasonably be claimed
How to judge value for money, efficiency, effectiveness and quality in business support
The monitoring and reporting requirements of the contracts and funding programmes you work on
Approaches to comparing support services with others, and using the results to improve them
How to handle complaints and problems with the support provided

standards.title: Apply current business knowledge
standards.evolvedFrom: Business Support 9 (Apply your knowledge and experience of business and its core functions); Business Information 8; Introduction to Enterprise Support 5; awareness-level content from Business Support 12 and 16; Business and Enterprise Support (2013) unit 7.
standards.summary: To be a good business support professional you need a broad, current understanding of the essential areas of business and how they link to and support each other. You also need practical knowledge of the competing demands, pressures and motivations facing the people who run businesses. This Standard sets the level of knowledge expected of every practitioner: enough to recognise issues across the whole business, see how they connect and know when specialist help is needed. The Specialist Standards set out greater depth in particular areas, for example finance (S1), AI and digital adoption (S3), sustainability (S7), people and skills (S8), start-up (S9) and growth and markets (S10).

performanceRequirements.text: Apply your knowledge of business, its core functions and how they link to and affect each other when working with clients
Apply your understanding of the pressures, motivations and emotional investment involved in running a business
Recognise when a problem presented in one area of the business is caused by another (for example a cash flow problem caused by poor marketing)
Keep your knowledge of business up to date, including changes in regulation, technology and the economy
Recognise when a client needs specialist or regulated advice and refer them to a suitably qualified professional

knowledgeRequirements.text: How to assess where a business stands, what its owners want for it and what it will take to succeed
How businesses plan, from simple action plans to full business plans

The core functions of a business (finance, customers and markets, people, operations and technology, sustainability, and legal and regulatory requirements) and how they affect each other, at a level sufficient to recognise issues in each and when specialist help is needed
How to keep track of regulatory change, where authoritative information is available, and when to refer to a professional adviser

The needs of different types of business, including the self-employed, home-based, micro, small, medium-sized and family businesses, social enterprises and co-operatives, and structured formats such as franchising, licensing, direct selling and distribution agreements
What businesses typically need at each stage, from pre-start and start-up through growth and maturity to difficulty, succession and exit
What running a business asks of the people who do it: the personal stake they have in it, the range of abilities it calls on, the risks they carry, and the time and energy it takes

standards.title: Practise ethically and professionally
standards.evolvedFrom: the ethical and professional guidelines referred to throughout the Business Support Standards (units 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 and 7); Business Support 11 (item h); Business and Enterprise Support (2013), the guidelines referred to in units 5, 10, 13 and 18, and unit 17 (in part).
standards.summary: This is about working to professional and ethical standards in everything you do. It covers integrity and impartiality, managing conflicts of interest, confidentiality and data protection, working within your competence and the limits of regulated activity, inclusive practice, safety and the responsible use of digital and AI tools. In the original standards, these were left to the guidelines of each organisation or professional body. They are now set out as part of the Standards themselves.

performanceRequirements.text: Act with honesty, integrity and impartiality, putting the client's interests first
Identify, declare and manage conflicts of interest, including commercial interests, referral arrangements and the pressure of programme targets
Keep client information confidential and handle personal data lawfully, securely and only for agreed purposes
Work within the limits of your competence and role, and within the boundaries of regulated activity (for example regulated financial or legal advice)
Treat all clients fairly, work inclusively, and make reasonable adjustments where a client needs them
Recognise ethical dilemmas and matters of professional conduct, and respond to them appropriately, seeking advice where needed
Use digital and AI tools responsibly in your practice: protect client information, check outputs for accuracy, and be open with clients about how you use them
Take reasonable steps to protect your own safety and that of your clients, including when meeting in person, working alone or visiting clients' premises
Follow the policies, codes of conduct and contractual requirements that apply to your work, and raise concerns where they conflict with the client's interests
Check your practice regularly against these Standards, relevant regulations and your professional and ethical obligations

knowledgeRequirements.text: The ethical principles of business support: integrity, impartiality, objectivity, confidentiality, competence and respect
What counts as a conflict of interest and how to manage one
The principles of data protection and your obligations when collecting, storing, sharing and deleting client information
The boundaries of regulated activity relevant to business support (for example regulated financial advice, credit broking, reserved legal activities and insolvency advice), and when to refer
Equality legislation, inclusive practice and reasonable adjustments
How AI and other digital tools can create risks to confidentiality, accuracy and fairness, and how to manage them
Health, safety and personal safety in client work, including lone working and online meetings
How to respond if you have concerns about the welfare of a client or someone connected with them
Complaints and whistleblowing procedures, and how to raise concerns
The professional codes and contractual requirements relevant to your work

standards.title: Develop own practice and networks
standards.evolvedFrom: Business Support 5 (Develop networks to provide access to information, support and resources); Business Support 6 (Evaluate the quality of your own practice in business support); Business Support 7 (Develop your own ability to provide business support); Business Information 5 to 7; Introduction to Enterprise Support 3; Business and Enterprise Support (2013) units 1 (in part), 12 (in part), 13, 17 and 18.
standards.summary: This is about disciplined reflection on your practice, continuing professional development and building the networks that make you a valued professional to work with. Whatever the focus of your practice, your aim should be to keep developing your ability to support clients, from a personal and career point of view and in line with the needs of the organisation you work for.

performanceRequirements.text: Review from time to time what your role requires of you and how that is changing
Reflect on your practice after client work and at key points, using valid evidence about your methods, their impact and the improvements needed
Seek honest feedback regularly from clients, colleagues and others who see your work
Assess your knowledge, skills and behaviours against these Standards and identify your development needs
Plan, do and record your continuing professional development, revising your plan as your role and practice change
Keep your knowledge of business practice and business support up to date, including developments in technology and policy
Develop professional networks, both formal and informal, that open up information, expertise and opportunities for you and your clients
Give to your networks as well as take from them, so that people trust you, and keep client confidences within them
Open up your contacts to clients where this creates opportunities for them
Evaluate the impact of your development activities and networks on the quality of the support you provide

knowledgeRequirements.text: Why reflective practice matters, how to do it, and why self-assessment alone can mislead
Sources of useful feedback on your practice (for example professional supervision, peer review, reflective practice groups and client feedback)
How to write a development plan with clear, measurable objectives and timescales
The strengths and limits of different ways of developing (for example courses, workshops, conferences, mentoring, peer learning, online learning and work shadowing)
How you learn best
How to grow and keep up networks, including through specialist groups, business networks and online professional communities
How to judge what your networks are worth to you and your clients, against the time they take
The CPD expectations that apply to you, including those of SFEDI and of your organisation or professional body
Your own values and motivations for working in business support, and how they affect your practice

standards.title: Business Finance and Funding
standards.whoFor: business support professionals who help clients understand their finances, plan financially and access finance.
standards.evolvedFrom: Business Support 9 (finance knowledge, items 4 to 9); Business Support 2 (knowledge items 7, 17 and 18); funding content in Business Support 1, 5, 10 and 14.
standards.summary: This is about helping clients understand their financial position, plan and forecast with confidence, and find and secure the right finance for their stage and circumstances. It includes knowing where general business guidance ends and regulated financial advice begins.

performanceRequirements.text: Help the client understand their financial statements and what they show about the health of the business
Use financial ratios and performance measures to interpret the client's financial information and identify trends, risks and opportunities
Help the client build cash flow forecasts and financial projections, and test the assumptions and scenarios behind them
Help the client understand their costs, pricing, margins and break-even point
Help the client identify their financing needs and the forms of finance suited to their stage, sector and circumstances
Help the client prepare to approach funders, including the plans, information and evidence funders expect
Explain the obligations, costs and risks of different forms of finance, including personal guarantees and giving up equity
Present financial findings and recommendations clearly to support the client's decisions
Recognise the limitations of financial analysis, and when the client needs an accountant, a regulated financial adviser or an insolvency professional
Recognise early signs of financial difficulty and help the client to act early

knowledgeRequirements.text: The profit and loss account, balance sheet and cash flow statement, and the financial terms used by small and medium-sized businesses
The relationship between profit, cash flow and forecasting, and how to manage working capital, credit control and late payment
Financial ratios and key performance indicators, and their limitations
Costing, pricing, margins and break-even analysis

The main forms of finance (for example grants, loans, overdrafts, asset and invoice finance, government-backed schemes, equity and angel investment, crowdfunding and community finance) and when each is suitable
What different funders look for, and how to prepare a business for investment
The basics of business taxation and digital tax requirements, and when to refer to an accountant
The boundaries of regulated activity in finance (for example regulated financial advice and credit broking) and how to work within them
The signs of financial distress and the sources of help available
Financial modelling and forecasting tools, including spreadsheets and accounting software

standards.title: Project and Programme Delivery
standards.whoFor: business support professionals who plan and deliver advisory projects, manage client caseloads, or run business support programmes.
standards.evolvedFrom: Business Support 11 (Manage a business support client portfolio); Business Support 3 (action planning); Business Support 8 (service-level monitoring).
standards.summary: This is about planning, managing and evaluating advisory projects and programmes so that they deliver for clients on time, within resources and in line with contractual and funding requirements. It includes managing a balanced caseload of clients and keeping their journeys moving.

performanceRequirements.text: Define the objectives, scope and success measures of an advisory project or programme
Produce a plan using appropriate project management tools, setting out milestones, resources and responsibilities
Plan and prioritise the resources needed, including your own time across a caseload
Identify and manage risks, issues, assumptions and dependencies during delivery
Monitor delivery against the plan and respond to change and shifting priorities while maintaining quality
Manage a balanced caseload of clients in line with programme objectives, with clear approaches for taking on clients, maintaining their progress and planning their exit
Keep stakeholders informed and manage their expectations
Meet the contractual, funding and reporting requirements of the project or programme, including requirements for data and evidence
Deliver programme targets only in ways that remain in the best interests of clients
Evaluate delivery against the plan, resources and timescales, and identify lessons learned to inform future work

knowledgeRequirements.text: The project lifecycle and common delivery approaches (for example linear, agile and hybrid), and when each is suitable
Planning tools and techniques (for example work breakdown, Gantt charts, responsibility matrices and task boards), including digital project tools
Risk, issue and change control techniques
Caseload management techniques, including managing client journeys, maintaining momentum and exit strategies
Stakeholder management and communication planning
Contract and funding compliance, including evidence, audit and data requirements
How to monitor and evaluate projects and programmes and capture lessons learned

standards.title: AI and Digital Adoption
standards.whoFor: business support professionals who help businesses adopt digital technology and artificial intelligence.
standards.evolvedFrom: new Standard. Builds on Business Support 9 (item 34, the use of technology to support business processes) and Business Support 7 (use of information and communications technology).
standards.summary: This is about helping businesses understand, choose, adopt and get value from digital technology and AI, safely and in proportion to their size and needs. It involves assessing where a business is now, identifying practical opportunities, managing the risks and building the skills needed. Professionals working to this Standard are expected to use these tools confidently in their own practice.

performanceRequirements.text: Assess the client's current digital capability, including skills, systems, data and attitudes to technology
Help the client identify where digital technology and AI could improve their processes, products, customer experience and decision making
Help the client prioritise opportunities by value, cost, risk and readiness, starting with practical, low-risk steps
Help the client build a business case and plan for adoption, covering skills, change management and how benefits will be measured
Help the client assess digital and AI products and suppliers impartially
Help the client identify and manage the risks of adoption, including data protection, cyber security, accuracy, bias, intellectual property and dependence on suppliers
Help the client develop simple, proportionate policies for the responsible use of AI in their business
Support the client to build digital and AI skills across the business, and direct them to appropriate training
Review with the client whether adoption has delivered the expected benefits
Demonstrate effective, practical use of digital and AI tools in your own practice

knowledgeRequirements.text: The digital technologies commonly used by businesses (for example cloud services, accounting and customer relationship management systems, e-commerce, automation, data and analytics, and collaboration tools)
What AI, including generative AI, can and cannot do, its common business uses, and how it works at a level sufficient to advise on it
Digital maturity models and diagnostic tools
How to assess the costs and benefits of technology, including total cost of ownership and productivity gains
Data protection, cyber security (including recognised certification schemes) and intellectual property issues in digital and AI adoption
The risks of AI (for example inaccurate outputs, bias, over-reliance and supplier lock-in) and how to reduce them
Change management and skills development for technology adoption, including bringing staff along
The sources of support, funding and training for digital adoption, and how to keep up to date with them
Regulatory developments that affect how businesses operate digitally (for example digital tax and e-invoicing requirements)
How to judge when, how and to what degree AI should be used for a given task, and how to help clients and their staff develop that judgement

standards.title: Enterprise Mentoring
standards.whoFor: volunteer and professional mentors supporting people who are starting or running businesses.
standards.evolvedFrom: Business Support 4 (modes of support); Business Support 19 (item j); Business Information 1 (knowledge items 4 and 5, on how clients take in information); Introduction to Enterprise Support 1 to 4; Business and Enterprise Support (2013) unit 20.
standards.summary: This is about supporting the development of a business owner through a mentoring relationship. The mentor brings their own experience and insight; the mentee sets the goals and makes the decisions. It involves contracting the relationship clearly, creating a safe space built on mutual trust, listening and questioning in ways that help the mentee reach their own insights, drawing on experience without imposing solutions, recognising when mentoring has become advice, and bringing the relationship to a planned close once it has served its purpose.

performanceRequirements.text: Explain to the mentee what mentoring involves, how it differs from advice, coaching and consultancy, and what it asks of them

Set up the relationship with the mentee: its purpose, ground rules, confidentiality, how often and where or how you will meet, how long it is likely to last, and what happens if a meeting cannot go ahead
Create a safe environment and a relationship of mutual trust and respect, taking account of the mentee's culture, background and ways of thinking and working, including neurodiversity
Agree which topics are within the scope of the relationship, and ask permission before exploring personal or sensitive areas
Listen with full attention to what the mentee says and what they leave unsaid, without judging, and check your understanding
Ask well-timed, open and curious questions that help the mentee explore issues and reach their own insights
Recognise the feelings, concerns and pressures behind what the mentee says, and respond with sensitivity
Draw on your own business experience, including mistakes as well as successes, through examples and stories that help the mentee learn, without imposing your own solutions
Offer information and ideas with patience and tact, at a pace and in a form the mentee can absorb and use
Encourage the mentee to use new points of view when evaluating their situation and options
Leave the mentee in charge of their own goals and decisions
Build the mentee's confidence, knowledge and skills so they can reach their goals and, in time, manage without a mentor
Notice when you have slipped from mentoring into giving advice, and decide what to do about it
Recognise when the mentee needs support beyond the mentoring relationship and help them access it
Keep appropriate records of the relationship, in line with data protection requirements
Review progress against the mentee's goals, and the value of the relationship, with the mentee at agreed points
Recognise when the relationship has served its purpose or is no longer adding value, and bring it to a planned close that reviews what has been achieved and agrees next steps
Use supervision or peer support, and feedback from mentees, to reflect on and improve your mentoring practice
Help the mentee look back at setbacks and plans that went wrong, and draw lessons from them

knowledgeRequirements.text: What enterprise mentoring is and its different forms (for example one-to-one, group, peer, reverse and online mentoring; voluntary and paid)
How mentoring compares with coaching, advising, consultancy and training, and when mentoring is the right form of support
The stages of a mentoring relationship, from contracting to closure, and how rapport develops as the relationship matures
Questioning techniques, including open, curious and challenging questions, and how to judge when to use them
The different levels of listening, from listening to reply to listening for meaning, feelings and what is left unsaid, and how attention and intention affect the quality of listening
How to recognise and respond to emotions in mentoring conversations, and how stress and pressure can affect business decisions
How people take in and process information differently, including neurodivergent people, and how to adapt the pace and form of what you share
How to use your own experience in mentoring: when to share it, how to use stories and examples (including mistakes), and the risk of imposing your own solutions
Feedback techniques, and the use of reflective practice and supervision in mentoring
The boundaries of the mentor's role, including how to avoid dependency and how to recognise when a relationship is no longer adding value
Ethical codes for mentoring, confidentiality, conflicts of interest, and what to do if confidentiality is breached
Matching mentors and mentees, and what makes a match work
The practical and personal safety considerations in arranging mentoring meetings, including online
How to measure the impact of mentoring
How mentoring programmes are designed, matched and quality assured

standards.title: Business Coaching
standards.whoFor: coaches working with business owners, managers and teams.
standards.evolvedFrom: Business Support 4 (coaching as a mode of support).
standards.summary: This is about helping business owners and managers to clarify their goals, raise their awareness, find their own solutions and act on them, through a structured coaching relationship. The coach's expertise lies in the process rather than in providing answers.

performanceRequirements.text: Explain the coaching approach and how it differs from other forms of support, and agree a coaching contract covering goals, process, confidentiality, duration and costs
Help the client clarify their goals and what success will look like
Use questioning and active listening to raise the client's awareness and help them generate options
Challenge the client's assumptions and limiting beliefs constructively
Select and use coaching models and tools suited to the client and the goal
Create a positive coaching experience that is welcoming, participative, non-judgemental and focused on action
Hold the client accountable for agreed actions while respecting their autonomy
Recognise when the client needs a different form of support (for example advice, training or therapeutic support) and refer them
Review progress and impact with the client
Use supervision to reflect on and improve your coaching practice

knowledgeRequirements.text: The principles of coaching and the evidence for its effectiveness
Coaching models (for example GROW) and tools
Questioning, listening, feedback and challenge techniques
Theories of motivation, goal setting and behaviour change
The boundary between coaching and counselling or therapy, and how to recognise mental health concerns
Contracting and ethics in coaching, including recognised professional codes
Coaching teams and leaders in small businesses
How to measure the impact of coaching

standards.title: Enterprise Training and Facilitation
standards.whoFor: trainers and facilitators who deliver learning to people starting or running businesses.
standards.evolvedFrom: Business Support 19 (Deliver enterprise training to small business clients); Business and Enterprise Support (2013) unit 21.
standards.summary: This is about delivering practical, flexible training and facilitation that suits business owners, in person and online. It sets out the skills and knowledge particularly needed when training aspiring and existing business owners, in addition to general training skills.

performanceRequirements.text: Identify the learning needs of business clients and design training that is practical, relevant and up to date
Design sessions and programmes with clear objectives, suited to adult learners, for delivery in person, online or both
Bring in real examples and case studies, from your own business experience and that of others, that participants can relate to
Set a tone in sessions that is welcoming, practical and positive, where participants feel safe to share their problems
Find out what problems participants are facing, show you understand them, and work solutions into the session where you can
Adjust the structure, content and delivery as you go to fit what participants need
Encourage and stretch participants through the session, so that they leave ready to act
Facilitate discussion and peer learning within groups
Notice when you have shifted into coaching, mentoring or advising, and adjust your delivery accordingly
Point participants to other people and organisations that can help them further
Evaluate training using participant feedback and outcomes, and improve it
Be honest when a participant asks something you cannot answer, and find out the answer afterwards

knowledgeRequirements.text: What running a business involves day to day, and how this affects people's ability to take part in learning
How adults learn, including experiential learning
Training design, including learning needs analysis, objectives, session plans and schemes of work
Facilitation techniques for groups, including online and hybrid groups
How to use technology in training, including online platforms and AI tools
Accessible and inclusive training practice
Why hearing from others who have overcome similar problems helps participants
Methods of evaluating training
Where your expertise ends and when to refer to other sources or people

standards.title: Sustainable Business and Net Zero
standards.whoFor: business support professionals who help businesses improve their environmental performance and respond to the move to net zero.
standards.evolvedFrom: Business Support 16 (Help the client to assess the environmental impact of their business).
standards.summary: This is about helping businesses understand their environmental impact and the requirements that apply to them, act on it in proportion to their size, and communicate their performance credibly. It covers compliance, carbon footprints, practical changes that cut costs, and responding to customers, supply chains, funders and public buyers.

performanceRequirements.text: Help the client identify the environmental laws, regulations and reporting requests that apply to their business and sector
Help the client assess their environmental impact, including energy use, emissions, waste, water and materials
Help the client establish a carbon footprint baseline using a recognised method suited to the size of the business
Identify practical changes that would reduce the client's environmental impact and costs, and investigate their costs and benefits
Help the client respond to sustainability requirements from customers, supply chains, funders and public procurement
Help the client identify climate-related risks and opportunities for the business, including new products and markets
Help the client build a proportionate plan with targets, responsibilities and review points
Help the client communicate their environmental commitments credibly and avoid misleading claims
Identify sources of advice, finance and incentives for environmental improvements
Encourage the client to review their environmental performance regularly and identify further improvements

knowledgeRequirements.text: The environmental laws and regulations affecting businesses (for example on emissions, waste, packaging, energy and water) and who enforces them
Net zero and what it means for small businesses, including the difference between direct emissions, emissions from purchased energy and supply chain emissions
Carbon accounting methods and tools suitable for small businesses
Energy efficiency, resource efficiency and circular economy principles
Sustainability requirements in supply chains and public procurement
The rules on environmental claims and how to avoid misleading customers
The physical and transition risks of climate change for businesses
Green finance and incentives, and how to keep up to date with them
The business benefits of good environmental practice, including cost savings, reputation, staff engagement, insurance and access to contracts
When to refer to specialist environmental or energy advisers

standards.title: People, Skills and Employment
standards.whoFor: business support professionals who help businesses recruit, manage and develop their people.
standards.evolvedFrom: Business Support 12 (Help the business to appreciate the link between improved business performance and the contribution of skills); Business Support 9 (HR and skills knowledge, items 21 to 31); Business and Enterprise Support (2013) unit 11.
standards.summary: This is about helping businesses see how their people and their skills contribute to performance, and helping them recruit, manage, develop and keep the people they need. It includes identifying skill gaps, matching needs to solutions and knowing when the business needs specialist HR or legal advice.

performanceRequirements.text: Find out what the client wants to achieve, and help them see how their people and their skills can get them there
Encourage the client to aim higher by investing in skills, including leadership and management skills
Use skills diagnostic tools with the client to find where the business is short of the skills it needs
Show the client what developing skills at every level of the business could be worth to them
Help the client find the right way to meet each skill need, including apprenticeships, training and funded programmes
Help the client plan recruitment, induction and retention
Help the client understand their obligations and good practice as an employer, and when to seek HR or legal advice
Help the client develop approaches to performance, reward and wellbeing that suit the size of the business
Help the client plan for workforce change, including growth, restructuring and the introduction of new technology
Review with the client the impact of people and skills development on the business

knowledgeRequirements.text: The link between skills, productivity and business performance
Skills diagnostic tools and training needs analysis
The skills and apprenticeship system, the funding available and how to access it, and how to keep up to date with changes
Recruitment and selection practice, including inclusive recruitment
The essentials of employment law and how to keep up to date with reforms, and when to refer
Supervision, appraisal, performance management, pay and reward
Leadership and management development for owner-managers
Workplace wellbeing and flexible working
Workforce planning

standards.title: Start-up and Self-employment Support
standards.whoFor: business support professionals who help people explore, plan and start a business or become self-employed.
standards.evolvedFrom: Business Support 9 (business experience, items 13 to 20, and items 37 and 38); Introduction to Enterprise Support 5; Business Information 8; Business and Enterprise Support (2013) units 5 and 19 (in part).
standards.summary: This is about helping people decide whether starting a business is right for them, test their ideas, plan and launch, and get through the early months of trading. It recognises the emotional investment and personal risk involved, and the different starting points people come from.

performanceRequirements.text: Help the individual explore their motivations, skills, circumstances and readiness for self-employment or starting a business
Help them develop their business idea and test it with potential customers before committing significant resources
Help them choose an appropriate legal form and understand their registration, tax and insurance obligations
Help them develop a proportionate business plan, including pricing, cash flow and break-even
Help them understand how starting a business may affect their benefits, employment and personal finances, and direct them to specialist advice
Help them identify start-up finance options and prepare applications
Help them plan their routes to market and first sales
Support them through the early months of trading, including record-keeping and cash management
Help them reach an informed decision where an idea is not viable
Adapt your support for under-represented founders, and for people starting from unemployment or alongside caring responsibilities

knowledgeRequirements.text: The steps in starting a business, and what it takes to start and run one successfully
Techniques for developing and testing business ideas (for example customer discovery and testing a value proposition)
Legal forms and registration requirements, and the basics of tax and insurance for new businesses
Start-up finance options
How self-employment interacts with benefits and employment status, and where to get specialist advice
The emotional investment, risk, time and commitment involved in starting a business
The barriers faced by under-represented founders and the tailored support available
The common causes of early-stage failure and how to reduce the risk
The particular needs of home-based and part-time businesses

standards.title: Growth, Productivity and International Trade
standards.whoFor: business support professionals who work with established businesses that want to grow, become more productive or trade internationally.
standards.evolvedFrom: Business Support 2 (business analysis); Business Support 9 (strategy, items 1 to 3, and business improvement tools, items 46 and 47); Business Information 1 (international trade information).
standards.summary: This is about helping established businesses to plan and manage growth, improve productivity, innovate and trade internationally. It includes strengthening leadership and management, finding the support and finance for growth, and managing the risks that growth brings.

performanceRequirements.text: Help the client assess their growth potential, ambition and capacity
Help the client develop a growth strategy and plan covering markets, products, people, systems and finance
Help the client identify and address constraints on productivity in operations, management and technology
Help the client strengthen leadership and management capability for growth
Help the client assess innovation opportunities and the support available for research and development
Help the client assess international opportunities, their readiness to trade internationally and the risks involved
Help the client understand the requirements of exporting and importing, including customs, documentation, regulations and payment
Help the client prepare to bid for and win public and private sector contracts
Identify sources of support and finance for growth, innovation and trade
Help the client manage the risks of growth, including cash flow pressure and overtrading

knowledgeRequirements.text: Growth strategies (for example market penetration, market development, product development and diversification)
Productivity measurement and improvement techniques (for example process improvement and benchmarking)
Leadership, management and organisational development for growing businesses
Innovation processes and the protection of intellectual property
The essentials of international trade, including market research, routes to market, customs and rules of origin, documentation, payment and currency risk, and trade agreements
Public procurement processes and how to bid
Finance for growth, including equity investment
The risks of rapid growth and overtrading
Business improvement tools and frameworks (for example quality and excellence models, balanced scorecards and people management standards) and business awards

standards.title: Supporting Businesses in Difficulty
standards.whoFor: business support professionals who work with businesses facing financial, operational or personal difficulty, or planning succession, sale or closure.
standards.evolvedFrom: new Standard. Builds on Business Support 1 (item e and knowledge item 8) and Business Support 9 (knowledge item 16).
standards.summary: This is about recognising when a business is in difficulty, raising it with the owner sensitively, and helping them act early and get the right help. It covers immediate steps to protect the business, recovery where it is viable, and decisions about succession, sale or closure. Much of the specialist help needed in this area is regulated, so knowing the limits of your role and referring promptly are central.

performanceRequirements.text: Recognise the early warning signs of business difficulty, whether financial, operational or personal
Raise your concerns with the client sensitively and help them face the situation
Help the client assess their position, including cash flow, debts, creditors and the options available
Help the client take immediate steps to protect cash and reduce risk
Direct the client promptly to debt advice, insolvency professionals, or legal and accounting help when they need it, within the limits of your role
Help the client prepare the information they need for discussions with creditors, lenders, landlords and tax authorities
Recognise signs of stress or poor mental health and direct the client to appropriate support
Help the client plan recovery or turnaround where the business is viable
Support the client through decisions about succession, sale or closure

knowledgeRequirements.text: The common causes and warning signs of business difficulty
Managing cash in a crisis, including credit control and late payment
The informal and formal options open to businesses in financial difficulty, at an awareness level, and who is qualified to advise on them
The duties of company directors when a company is in financial difficulty, at an awareness level
The free debt advice and wellbeing support available to business owners
Mental health awareness and how to direct people to support
Succession planning, selling a business and planned closure
The boundaries of your role and of regulated activity in this area

standards.title: Social Enterprise and Community Business
standards.whoFor: business support professionals who work with social enterprises, co-operatives, charities that trade and community businesses.
standards.evolvedFrom: the social enterprise content throughout the Business Support Standards (for example Business Support 2, knowledge items 12, 13 and 24, and Business Support 9, item 45).
standards.summary: This is about supporting enterprises that trade for a social or environmental purpose. It involves helping them balance mission and financial sustainability, choose the right legal and governance structure, find suitable finance and evidence their social impact.

performanceRequirements.text: Help the client clarify their social or environmental mission and how their business model delivers it
Help the client choose an appropriate legal and governance structure
Help the client develop a business model that balances mission and financial sustainability
Help the client identify funding and finance options, including grants, social investment and community shares
Help the client strengthen their governance, including the role of the board and the involvement of volunteers
Help the client measure and report their social impact
Help the client win contracts, including public contracts that take account of social value
Help the client engage their community and stakeholders

knowledgeRequirements.text: How social enterprises compare with private businesses, including the triple bottom line

The legal forms available to social enterprises (for example community interest companies, charities, co-operatives, community benefit societies and companies limited by guarantee) and how they are regulated
Governance, and the responsibilities of directors, trustees and members
Social investment and community finance
Approaches to measuring social impact
Social value in public procurement
Mission drift, asset locks and the balance between trading and purpose
Working with volunteers

standards.title: Professional Services for Small Businesses
standards.whoFor: business consultants, accountants, bookkeepers, solicitors, bank staff, insurers and other professionals who provide services to small businesses.
standards.evolvedFrom: Business Support 18 (Deliver professional services that give added value to small business clients); Business and Enterprise Support (2013) unit 22.
standards.summary: This is about delivering a flexible and proactive professional service that suits each small business client, and adds value beyond the technical service itself. It can be used by anyone delivering professional services to small businesses, including consultancy.

performanceRequirements.text: Show small business clients that you understand businesses like theirs, drawing on your experience of working with or in them
Get to know each client and what they want from working with you
Learn about the client's business, its market, how it works and what affects it
Find out what the client already knows about your technical area, and fill the gaps in terms they can use
Put forward practical, workable options that will benefit the client
Before starting any work, set out clearly what it involves, how long it will take and what it will cost
Leave decisions about which of your services to buy firmly with the client
Point out where the client could work more effectively, with the likely benefits and costs
Refer the client to other experts and to business support when their services may help
Collect and use client feedback to improve your service

knowledgeRequirements.text: What running a small business demands day to day
How business owners' outlook can differ from that of employees (for example in how they view risk)
The rules and requirements in your field that apply to small businesses at each stage of their development
Where your core service could usefully stretch to cover related issues that matter to small business clients
How to put technical language into plain terms
How to set prices that small businesses can afford
Why it pays to look at the client's longer-term needs and to build their own capability
How much small business owners rely on personal recommendation
The other professionals and support services that work well alongside yours
Frameworks and tools for identifying the improvements a client has made after an assignment

standards.title: Designing and Commissioning Business Support
standards.whoFor: people in government departments, combined and local authorities, agencies and funders who design, commission, procure or manage business support.
standards.evolvedFrom: Business Support 17 (Develop or deliver policies or programmes that help small businesses).
standards.summary: This is about conceiving, specifying, procuring, designing, delivering and evaluating policies and programmes that meet their objectives and genuinely help the businesses they are designed for. It includes specifying and assuring the quality of the advisers and providers who deliver them.

performanceRequirements.text: Use recent and credible evidence about businesses and their needs when developing policies and programmes
Consult business owners, and people with business support expertise, on draft policies, programmes and materials
Make sure policies and programmes address issues that are important to businesses and can be combined flexibly to fit the needs of different businesses
Make support easy to find and access, keeping steps, repeated requests for information and bureaucracy to a minimum
Set costs and eligibility rules that are realistic for businesses and do not discourage them from taking part
Make sure policies, programmes and materials are in plain English and free of jargon
Specify the quality of support required, including the competence of the advisers who deliver it, and how it will be assured
Set aims, measures and evaluation that focus on outcomes for businesses rather than outputs or targets alone
Monitor programmes in ways that keep the focus on businesses' needs as well as audit requirements
Link programmes to the wider support landscape so that businesses can move easily between services

knowledgeRequirements.text: What people running businesses deal with day to day, and what motivates them
How policies, systems and requirements appear to someone running a business
Where to find recent and credible research about businesses and business support
Outcome-focused programme design, including theories of change and logic models
Procurement and grant funding processes, including subsidy control rules
Evaluation methods for public programmes
How to specify and assure the quality of advisers and providers, including the use of recognised standards and qualifications
The local, national and sector networks that programmes can link to
How to gain first-hand understanding of what it is like to run a small business (for example by shadowing or working in one)

standards.title: Rural and Land-based Business
standards.whoFor: business support professionals working with farms, estates and other land-based businesses, and with businesses based in rural areas.
standards.evolvedFrom: new Standard. Builds on Business Support 7 (developing practice in particular business sectors) and Business Support 9 (specific industry sectors and business models).
standards.summary: This is about supporting farms, estates and other rural and land-based businesses in ways that fit how they work. It involves taking a whole-business and whole-family view, starting from a clear baseline, and helping clients make practical, affordable changes, including diversification, responding to changes in farm support and planning for succession.

performanceRequirements.text: Take a whole-business and, where relevant, whole-family view of the client, including how the household, the land and the business affect each other
Establish a clear baseline of the business's position at the outset, using benchmarking against similar businesses where it is available
Help the client set their own goals and plan changes that are practical, affordable and achievable alongside their working patterns, seasons and capacity

Help the client assess diversification opportunities (for example tourism, food and drink, renewable energy, property and new land uses), including how they fit with the core business and their planning, licensing, tenancy and tax implications
Help the client understand and respond to changes in farm and land-use support and regulation

Help the client assess opportunities in markets for environmental goods and services (for example biodiversity net gain, carbon and nature schemes), including the long-term commitments and risks involved
Help the client overcome constraints common in rural areas, including digital connectivity, transport, access to markets, planning, energy supply and recruiting and housing staff
Use peer learning, discussion groups and practical, on-site learning alongside one-to-one support, where these will help the client
Help the client plan for succession early, including involving the next generation and addressing family and ownership issues
Help the client find and access rural, sector and general sources of finance and support, and keep in contact to help them maintain progress
Help the client work with other local businesses and community organisations, including through collaboration, co-operatives and community-owned enterprises
Recognise signs of isolation, stress or financial pressure, and direct the client to specialist rural support

knowledgeRequirements.text: The structure of the rural economy and the range of rural businesses, including farming, forestry, food and drink, tourism, creative and home-based businesses
The particular constraints facing rural businesses (for example connectivity, transport, planning, grid capacity, housing, skills and access to finance) and the support available to address them
The economics of farm and land-based businesses, including enterprise costings, benchmarking, and the effects of seasonality, weather and commodity prices
Farm and land-use support schemes and regulation, how they are changing, and how to keep up to date with them
Diversification options and the planning, licensing, tax, insurance and tenancy issues they raise
Markets for environmental goods and services, and how natural capital can be valued and traded
Land ownership and tenancy arrangements, and how they affect business decisions
Family business dynamics and succession planning in farming and other rural businesses
Effective approaches to rural business support, including peer groups, discussion groups, demonstration and on-farm learning combined with one-to-one support
Community businesses, co-operatives and other models of rural collaboration
Sources of specialist rural support, including rural support charities, land agents and sector bodies

standards.title: Creative Industries
standards.whoFor: business support professionals working with creative businesses, creative freelancers and cultural organisations, across sectors such as advertising, architecture, crafts, design, fashion, film, television, games, music, performing and visual arts, publishing, and museums and galleries.
standards.evolvedFrom: new Standard. Builds on Business Support 7, which identified creative businesses as an area of sector practice, and Business Support 9 (item 52, intellectual property).
standards.summary: This is about helping creative businesses, freelancers and cultural organisations to protect and earn from their intellectual property, build sustainable business models, manage irregular income, plan and fund projects, and connect with the networks and specialist support around them.

performanceRequirements.text: Understand the client's creative practice, values and motivations, and work with them in ways that respect their creative autonomy alongside their commercial goals
Help the client identify, protect, manage and earn from their intellectual property, including through licensing, royalties and contracts
Help the client develop a sustainable business model, which may combine commissions, projects, products, licensing, teaching, grants and other income

Help freelancers and portfolio workers manage irregular income, set their rates, agree contracts, deal with late payment, and plan for tax and pensions, recognising the unpaid time spent pitching and on administration
Help the client plan and cost creative, research and development, and innovation projects before they apply for funding
Help the client identify and access sector-specific finance, including public funding, investment, crowdfunding and creative industry tax reliefs, and prepare strong applications
Help the client negotiate collaborations, co-productions and commissions, including how intellectual property and income will be shared
Help the client reach audiences and markets, including through digital distribution, platforms and international markets
Help the client assess the opportunities and risks that AI and other new technologies pose for their creative work and their intellectual property
Connect the client with creative networks, clusters, freelancer communities and specialist sector support, building on what already exists locally
Help cultural and not-for-profit creative organisations strengthen their governance, resilience and investment readiness

knowledgeRequirements.text: The make-up of the creative industries and their sub-sectors, and how business models differ between them
The role of freelancers and micro businesses in the creative workforce, and the particular pressures they face
Intellectual property, including copyright, design rights, trade marks, patents and moral rights; licensing; collective management organisations; and how rights are enforced
How to value and use intangible assets, including when raising finance

Creative industry funding and finance, including public funders, specialist investors, and creative industry tax reliefs and expenditure credits (for example for film, television, video games, theatre, orchestras and exhibitions)
Contracts used in creative work, including commissions, licences, fees and the assignment of rights
Fair work and payment practices for freelancers, and the protections available against late payment
How AI is changing creative production and distribution, and the current position on copyright and AI
Audience development and digital distribution
Creative clusters, networks and specialist support, and how to keep up to date with them
The barriers to diversity and inclusion in the creative workforce, and how support can address them

standards.title: Business Resilience
standards.whoFor: business support professionals who help businesses prepare for, withstand, recover from and adapt to disruption.
standards.evolvedFrom: new Standard. Builds on Business Support 2 (knowledge item 8, risk assessment) and Business Support 3 (knowledge item 22, contingency planning). S17 is about preparing for and adapting to disruption; S11 (Supporting Businesses in Difficulty) covers what to do once a business is already in difficulty.
standards.summary: This is about helping businesses understand the risks that matter most to them, put proportionate plans in place that grow with the business, and learn and adapt after every disruption. It covers the operational, financial, digital and people sides of a business, and the personal resilience of the owner.

performanceRequirements.text: Help the client identify the risks and potential disruptions most relevant to their business, using national, local and sector risk information
Help the client identify their critical activities, people, suppliers, customers, systems and data, and the impact of losing each of them

Help the client develop a business continuity plan, proportionate to the size of the business, that sets out how they would keep critical activities going and recover, starting simply and building over time
Help the client strengthen their financial resilience, including cash reserves, access to credit, appropriate insurance and reducing dependence on a few customers or suppliers
Help the client strengthen the resilience of their supply chain, including alternative suppliers and stock levels
Help the client put basic cyber security and data backup measures in place, and plan how they would respond to and recover from a cyber incident
Help the client prepare for physical risks, including extreme weather, flooding, fire and the loss of power or premises
Help the client reduce their dependence on key people, including through documented processes, cross-training and succession arrangements
