Help the client plan how they would communicate with staff, customers, suppliers and others during a disruption
Encourage the client to test and review their plans regularly and after any incident, and to act on the lessons learned
Help the owner build their personal resilience, including managing pressure, workload and isolation, and direct them to wellbeing support where needed
Help the client recognise early signs of longer-term change in their market or environment, and adapt their business model in response

knowledgeRequirements.text: What business resilience means: the ability to anticipate, prepare for, respond to, recover from and adapt to disruption
The main types of risk facing businesses, and sources of risk information, including national risk assessments and sector research
Risk assessment and business impact analysis techniques suitable for small businesses
The principles of business continuity planning, recognised standards and good practice (for example ISO 22301), and how to apply them in proportion to the size of the business
Financial resilience, including cash buffers, credit facilities, insurance (including business interruption cover) and the risks of depending on a few customers
Supply chain risk and how to reduce it

The basic cyber security controls small businesses need (for example backing up data, protecting against malware, keeping devices secure, using strong passwords and recognising phishing) and how to respond to an incident
Physical and climate-related risks, including flood preparedness, and how businesses can adapt to them
Key person risk and succession arrangements
How to communicate during and after a disruption
Personal resilience and wellbeing for business owners, including the effects of pressure, isolation and fear of failure, and the support available
How resilience planning links to support for businesses in difficulty (S11), and when to refer

standards.title: Developing Enterprising Skills
standards.whoFor: business support professionals, enterprise coaches, and employability and youth workers who help people develop enterprising skills, whether or not they go on to start a business.
standards.evolvedFrom: Business and Enterprise Support (2013) unit 19 (Support the client through developing personal enterprising skills) and unit 1 (developing creativity and innovation in others). S18 is about enterprising skills for any path; S9 (Start-up and Self-employment Support) covers starting a business.
standards.summary: This is about helping people develop the attributes, behaviours and skills that make them enterprising: spotting opportunities, generating and testing ideas, thinking creatively, making the most of the resources they already have, and taking measured risks. These skills matter in employment and study as well as in starting a business, so this Standard applies whatever path the individual chooses.

performanceRequirements.text: Help the individual consider how being enterprising could help them reach their goals, whether in employment, self-employment, study or starting a business
Help the individual take stock of how enterprising they are, recognising strengths and areas to develop
Help the individual spot opportunities and generate ideas, and understand how an opportunity differs from an idea
Encourage the individual to think creatively and try new approaches when developing and testing their ideas
Help the individual list the resources they already have (for example skills, knowledge, contacts, time and money) and work out what more they would need
Help the individual separate their technical or trade abilities from their business management abilities, and plan how to fill any gaps
Help the individual understand what they could put at risk, financially, personally and socially, in pursuing an opportunity, and how to keep that risk in proportion
Help the individual map out the main challenges, actions and milestones between an idea and putting it into action
Connect the individual with people, networks and programmes that can help them build their enterprising skills

knowledgeRequirements.text: What it means to be enterprising, the attributes, behaviours and skills involved, and frameworks that describe them
Why enterprising skills matter in employment, self-employment and study
Ways of assessing how enterprising someone is
How people spot opportunities, where ideas come from, and how to give constructive feedback on an idea
Techniques for developing creativity and innovation in others
Approaches to assessing personal and business resources, including starting from the resources a person already has
The difference between being good at a trade or craft and being able to manage a business
The financial, personal and social risks of acting on an idea, and how to manage them
How informal and formal networks help people find the resources they need
The barriers people face in developing enterprising skills, and the support available

standards.title: Business Model and Value Proposition Design
standards.whoFor: business support professionals who help businesses design, test and improve their business models and value propositions, using visual tools such as canvases.
standards.evolvedFrom: new Standard. Builds on Business and Enterprise Support (2013) unit 5 (knowledge items 16 to 19, business models and business plans) and unit 19 (item P5, a framework for the building blocks of a business model), and on Business Support 2 (business analysis). S9 and S18 use these tools when starting a business and developing enterprising skills; S19 covers their use in depth, for any business.
standards.summary: This is about helping business owners set out how their business creates, delivers and earns from value, and how well what they offer meets their customers' needs. It involves using visual tools such as the Business Model Canvas and the Value Proposition Canvas to generate and test ideas as well as analyse what already exists, and helping clients become confident using them for themselves.

performanceRequirements.text: Explain to the client what business model and value proposition tools are for, and how they can help a business of their size and stage
Choose tools suited to the client's situation, purpose and confidence, and adapt how you use them for the client

Help the client set out their current business model on one page, covering their customers, the value they offer, channels, customer relationships, revenue, key resources, activities, partners and costs
Help the client understand their customers' jobs, problems and hoped-for gains, using evidence rather than assumption
Help the client describe how their products and services relieve those problems and create those gains, and judge how well they fit
Use the tools to generate new ideas for products, services, customers and ways of earning revenue, as well as to analyse what already exists
Help the client identify the assumptions their business model and value proposition depend on, and rank them by risk and uncertainty
Help the client design simple, low-cost tests of their riskiest assumptions with real customers, and interpret the results
Help the client compare alternative business models and value propositions, including their costs, risks and sustainability
Help the client turn the agreed model into priorities and actions, and link it to their financial plans
Facilitate the use of the tools with teams, partners or groups, in person and online
Encourage the client to revisit their business model and value proposition as the business and its market change, and build their confidence to use the tools on their own

knowledgeRequirements.text: What a business model and a value proposition are, and how they differ from a business plan
The building blocks of a business model and how they affect each other

Recognised visual tools for business model and value proposition design (for example the Business Model Canvas and the Value Proposition Canvas), their strengths and limits, and the terms on which they can be used
How to understand customer needs, including customer segments, the jobs customers are trying to get done, their problems and the gains they want
What makes a good fit between a value proposition and customer needs, and how to evidence it
Techniques for generating new business models and value propositions, including starting from the value created for customers
How to identify, prioritise and test assumptions (for example customer interviews, prototypes, landing pages and pilot sales), and how to read the evidence
Common business model patterns (for example subscription, freemium, marketplace, licensing and social enterprise models) and when they fit
How business model choices affect costs, revenue, cash flow and risk
How to adapt the tools for social enterprises, the self-employed and very small businesses
Facilitation techniques for canvas-based workshops, in person and online, including digital whiteboards

standards.title: Consultative Advisory Practice
standards.whoFor: business advisers, account managers and consultants who hold diagnostic and developmental conversations with business owners and leaders, and want to deepen their consultative practice.
standards.evolvedFrom: Business Support 2 (Help the client to analyse the business and decide the way forward); Business Support 3 (Enable clients to implement changes in their business); Business Support 4 (Encourage clients to act for themselves); Business and Enterprise Support (2013) units 2, 6 and 22. C2 and C3 set out the diagnosis and support for change that every practitioner provides; S20 covers consultative practice in depth. S13 covers delivering a technical professional service to small businesses.
standards.summary: This is about holding conversations that uncover what a business really needs, challenge constructively and lead to actions the client owns. It involves preparing well, questioning and listening in depth, testing assumptions, influencing without taking over, and making sure advice serves both the business and the objectives of the programme it is delivered through.

performanceRequirements.text: Prepare for each conversation by researching the business, its sector and its history with the service, and planning what you want to find out
Open each conversation with a clear purpose, agree how the time will be used, and invite the client to set out what matters to them
Use questioning, listening and reflecting back to move from the issue the client presents to their underlying needs, constraints and opportunities
Test the client's assumptions and your own, separating what is known from what is believed
Challenge the client constructively, at the right moment and with evidence, while keeping the relationship strong
Recognise when the client is resisting, and explore the reasons behind it rather than pressing your own view
Help the client see the consequences of acting and of not acting, and reach decisions they own
Influence the client towards action using evidence, examples and options, without taking the decision from them
Agree specific actions at the end of each conversation, with who will do what and by when, and confirm them in writing where appropriate
Adapt your consultative style to the client, the issue and the stage of the relationship, moving between advising, facilitating and challenging as needed
Explain to the client how the support fits the objectives of the programme it is delivered through, and make sure your advice serves the client's needs as well as those objectives
Use self-assessment, observation and feedback on your conversations, and reflection, to improve your consultative practice

knowledgeRequirements.text: What makes an advisory approach consultative, and how it differs from providing information or giving instructions
Structures and planning tools for diagnostic and developmental conversations
Questioning techniques (for example open, probing, hypothetical, scaling and reflective questions), and how to sequence them
Levels of listening, and how to listen for meaning, feeling and what is left unsaid
How to distinguish the issue a client presents from their underlying needs, and the common reasons the two differ
Approaches to challenge and influence, including the balance between support and challenge, and how to challenge without damaging trust
How people respond to challenge and change, including defensiveness and resistance, and how to work with them
Cognitive biases that affect business decisions and advisory judgement (for example confirmation bias and optimism bias)
Logic models and theories of change in business support, and how individual interventions contribute to programme outcomes and policy objectives
Tools that support consultative practice (for example question banks, conversation planners, self-assessments and reflective journals)
How to use observation, peer review and feedback to develop consultative skills, including obtaining consent where conversations are observed or recorded

standards.title: Action Learning Facilitation
standards.whoFor: business support professionals who set up and facilitate action learning sets for business owners, advisers or mentors, and those who use action learning skills in their one-to-one work.
standards.evolvedFrom: new Standard. Builds on Business Support 19 (Deliver enterprise training to small business clients), Business Support 6 (Evaluate the quality of your own practice in business support) and Business and Enterprise Support (2013) unit 21. S6 covers enterprise training and facilitation in general; S21 covers action learning in depth.
standards.summary: This is about setting up and facilitating action learning sets, in which a small group meets regularly to work on real problems by questioning rather than advising. It includes facilitating in person and online, developing members so that sets can facilitate themselves, developing other facilitators, and using action learning skills in one-to-one work.

performanceRequirements.text: Explain what action learning is, how it works and what it asks of members, and agree whether it suits the people and the purpose involved
Set up a set, agreeing its purpose, membership, size, how often and how long it will meet, and whether it will meet in person or online
Agree ground rules with the set, including confidentiality, commitment, how time is shared and how members will question rather than advise
Help each presenter set out a real issue that they own and want to act on
Model and encourage open, insightful questions that help the presenter think differently, and steer members away from offering advice or solutions too early
Manage time, energy and participation so that every member presents and contributes
Help each presenter commit to actions, and at the next meeting help them review what they did and what they learned
Facilitate reflection on the process as well as the issues, so that members learn how they learn
Recognise and handle difficulties in a set, such as dominant or silent members, rescuing, advice giving and lapses in commitment
Adapt your facilitation for online and hybrid sets, maintaining participation and trust
Develop members' questioning, listening and facilitation skills so that the set can facilitate itself over time
Use action learning skills, such as questioning, listening and holding back from advice, in your one-to-one advisory and mentoring conversations
Support others to become action learning facilitators, including through co-facilitation, observation and feedback
Evaluate the value of a set to its members and their businesses, and act on what you learn

knowledgeRequirements.text: The principles of action learning, and how it differs from training, mentoring, coaching and other peer groups
The structure of an action learning set, and the roles of presenter, members and facilitator
Questioning approaches suited to action learning, and how a genuine question differs from advice phrased as a question
Listening and reflective practice, and how they support learning from experience
Group dynamics, and how to build trust and psychological safety in a group
The common difficulties in sets and how to handle them
Online and hybrid facilitation techniques and tools
How to move a set from facilitated to self-facilitated, and when this is appropriate
How to adapt action learning for business owners with limited time, and for members from different backgrounds and cultures
How to evaluate action learning, including its effect on members' practice and on their businesses
Confidentiality and ethics in group work, including what to do if confidentiality is broken

standards.title: Business Account Management
standards.whoFor: business support professionals who manage an ongoing relationship with a portfolio of businesses on behalf of a service, often coordinating support from several teams or organisations around each one.
standards.evolvedFrom: Business Support 1 (Maintain effective business support relationships with clients); Business Support 10 (Broker clients to business support services); Business Support 11 (Manage a business support client portfolio); Business and Enterprise Support (2013) units 4 and 14. S2 covers managing a caseload within a programme; S22 covers the longer-term relationship with each business and the coordination of support around it.
standards.summary: This is about building a trusted, long-term relationship with each business in a portfolio and making sure the right support reaches it at the right time. It involves account planning, using data and intelligence to understand each business, and coordinating colleagues, partners and specialists as one team around its needs.

performanceRequirements.text: Agree with the business how the account relationship will work, including the main contacts on both sides, how often you will be in touch and what the business can expect from the service
Build relationships across the business, not only with the owner or chief executive, while respecting who makes decisions
Develop an in-depth understanding of the business's strategy, performance, ambitions, challenges and decision makers
Prepare and keep up to date an account plan with the business, setting out its priorities, the support planned, who is involved and how progress will be reviewed
Use data and intelligence from client records, management information, published sources and conversations to understand each account and anticipate its needs
Coordinate colleagues, partners and specialists as one team around the business, making clear who leads, who does what and how information is shared
Make sure the business experiences joined-up support, without repeated requests for the same information or conflicting advice
Put the business's interests first when deciding what support to offer, including when this does not suit programme targets or your organisation's own services
Prioritise your time and effort across a portfolio of accounts according to need, potential and agreed service levels
Identify opportunities and risks for the business early, and raise them with the business and the right colleagues
Review the value of the relationship with the business regularly, and act on its feedback
Record account activity, contacts and outcomes accurately, so that colleagues can pick up the relationship, in line with data protection requirements
Plan for changes in the relationship, including handover to another account manager and the planned end of account management

knowledgeRequirements.text: The principles of account management and how they apply in business support, including how account management differs from managing a caseload
Account planning tools and techniques, including mapping relationships and stakeholders within a business
How businesses make decisions, and the roles and influence of owners, directors, managers and their advisers

Sources of data and intelligence about businesses (for example client relationship management records, company information, financial data and sector intelligence), and how to analyse them for insight into an account
How to use client relationship management systems to record, share and review account activity
How to coordinate support across teams and organisations, including referral agreements, information sharing and consent
Methods of segmenting and prioritising a portfolio of accounts
How to judge the health and value of an account relationship, including through client feedback and outcomes
How to manage conflicts between the business's interests, programme targets and your organisation's commercial interests
The data protection requirements for holding and sharing information about businesses and the people in them

standards.title: Digital Marketing and Social Media
standards.whoFor: business support professionals who build their own professional presence online, promote business support services, or help businesses market themselves through digital and social channels.
standards.evolvedFrom: new Standard. Builds on Business Support 9 (marketing and sales knowledge) and Business and Enterprise Support (2013) unit 1 (developing awareness amongst potential clients). C1 covers explaining your offer to potential clients, and C6 sets the business knowledge expected of every practitioner; S23 covers digital marketing and social media in depth.
standards.summary: This is about using digital and social channels well: building a credible professional presence, planning and creating content for the right audiences, testing and adapting, and using analytics to show results. It applies to professionals marketing their own practice or service, and to those helping clients market their businesses.

performanceRequirements.text: Identify the priority audiences for your practice, your service or the client's business, and where and how they use digital and social channels
Build and maintain a credible professional presence online that is consistent with your role, your organisation's policies and these Standards
Set clear objectives for digital and social activity that link to business or service outcomes
Plan content across channels, balancing what the audience values with what you or the client want to achieve
Create clear, accessible content in formats suited to each channel, including text, images and video
Work in short cycles, testing approaches, learning from the results and adapting content and channels quickly
Engage with audiences in ways that build trust, including responding to comments and messages and handling criticism constructively
Use analytics to measure reach, engagement and conversion, and to show the value of activity against its objectives
Plan and manage digital and social activity efficiently, using scheduling, templates and AI tools where appropriate, and checking AI-generated content for accuracy before it is published
Protect client confidentiality, and obtain consent before featuring clients, their businesses or their results
Help the client develop a proportionate digital marketing plan suited to their size, resources and skills
Help the client assess digital marketing products, platforms and suppliers impartially
Make sure your own and your clients' marketing follows the rules on advertising, endorsements, online reviews, electronic marketing and data protection

knowledgeRequirements.text: The main digital and social channels used by businesses and business support, and the audiences and purposes each suits
How to build a professional reputation online, and the risks to it
Content strategy and planning, including content calendars and reusing content across channels
Writing and designing for digital channels, including accessible content
Agile marketing approaches, including testing, measuring and iterating
Engaging and managing online communities, including handling negative feedback
Digital marketing analytics, the main measures and their limitations, and how to link them to business outcomes
Search, online advertising and email marketing, at a level sufficient to advise on them
Tools for planning, scheduling, creating and measuring content, including the responsible use of AI

The rules that apply to digital marketing, including advertising standards, endorsements and influencer marketing, online reviews, consent for electronic marketing and data protection, and where authoritative guidance is available
Social media policies, and the boundary between personal and professional use

standards.title: Inclusive Engagement with Under-represented Businesses
standards.whoFor: business support professionals, outreach staff and service managers who want to reach, engage and support business owners and entrepreneurs from communities that are under-represented in business support, including ethnic minority entrepreneurs.
standards.evolvedFrom: new Standard. Builds on Business Support 1 (Maintain effective business support relationships with clients), Business Support 5 (Develop networks to provide access to information, support and resources) and Business and Enterprise Support (2013) units 1 and 3. The professional behaviours (B10) and the Core Standards (C1, C3 and C7) set out the inclusive practice every practitioner shows; S24 covers inclusive engagement in depth.
standards.summary: This is about understanding who a service reaches and who it misses, building trust with under-represented communities, adapting how support is communicated and delivered, and learning from evidence what works. Working one to one with neurodivergent and disabled clients is covered in depth by S26 and S27.

performanceRequirements.text: Use data to find out which groups and areas the service reaches and which it misses, by comparing engagement with the business population it serves
Build relationships with community organisations, faith and cultural groups, business networks and other trusted intermediaries close to under-represented communities
Promote support through the channels, languages, places and voices that under-represented communities use and trust
Go to where people are, including community venues and events, rather than relying on people coming to the service
Find out about the experiences, aspirations and priorities of business owners from under-represented communities, including their past experience of support
Identify the barriers that stop people engaging, such as awareness, trust, language, eligibility rules, cost, time and the way support is designed
Recognise how culture, faith, family and community can shape how people run their businesses and make decisions, without making assumptions about individuals
Reflect on your own assumptions and biases, and how they may affect whom you engage and how
Adapt your communication, including language, pace, format and style, to the person you are working with, using interpreters or translated materials where needed
Build trust over time through consistent, reliable contact and by following through on what you offer
Adapt how support is delivered (for example timing, location, format, and group or one-to-one) to remove barriers to taking part
Connect clients with role models, peers, mentors and networks, including those from their own communities, as well as with mainstream support
Raise with your organisation the parts of service design, eligibility or process that create barriers, and suggest changes
Collect equality monitoring information lawfully and sensitively, explaining why it is asked for and respecting people's choice not to give it
Evaluate whether engagement and outcomes are improving for under-represented groups, and share what works and what does not
Use case studies and client feedback, with clients' consent, to improve your own practice and that of your colleagues and service

knowledgeRequirements.text: Which groups are under-represented in business ownership and in the use of business support, the evidence on why, and how to keep up to date with it
The make-up of the business population and communities in the areas you serve, and sources of local and national data on them, including official statistics
How to analyse engagement data by group and by area, including mapping, and the limits of what the data can show
The barriers to taking part in business support, including awareness, trust, language, digital access, eligibility, finance and the design of support

How culture, faith, family, community and migration can shape business practice, finance (for example faith-based approaches to borrowing and interest) and decision making, and the risk of stereotyping
Adaptive communication, including plain language, working with interpreters and communicating across cultures
Community engagement approaches, including working with trusted intermediaries, community leaders and networks
Unconscious bias and cultural humility, and how to reflect on your own practice
Equality legislation as it applies to business support services, including the difference between lawful positive action and unlawful positive discrimination
The data protection requirements for equality monitoring information, including the extra protection for special category data such as racial or ethnic origin
How to develop case studies and evidence of what works, with consent
Sources of specialist support for under-represented entrepreneurs, including community, sector and national organisations

standards.title: Brokering Specialist Support
standards.whoFor: business advisers, account managers and brokers who help businesses specify, choose, fund and work with consultants, trainers and other specialist providers, including on programmes that broker or fund specialist support.
standards.evolvedFrom: Business Support 13 (Help the client to critically assess a business support service provider's offer); Business Support 14 (Broker deals with business support service providers); Business Support 15 (in part); Business and Enterprise Support (2013) units 15 and 16 (in part). C4 covers finding, explaining and referring to support, which every practitioner does; S25 covers brokering in depth.
standards.summary: This is about helping clients turn a need into a clear brief, find and compare specialist providers, work out how to pay, agree clear terms and get value from the work, while the client keeps the decisions. It also covers working within the rules that apply when support is publicly funded.

performanceRequirements.text: Help the client set out what they need and write a brief that will draw realistic, comparable proposals from providers
Identify suitable providers and invite proposals, in line with any rules attached to public funding
Help the client decide how they will choose between providers, judging fit, quality and value, and taking account of any rules attached to public funding
Help the client test providers' offers, including checking references and understanding what their quality marks and accreditations show
Help the client work out how to pay for the support they need, including where putting in their own money unlocks other help
Help the client agree clear terms with the chosen provider, covering what will be delivered, by when, at what cost and how success will be judged
Help the client and providers understand each other, explaining jargon in both directions
Help the client and the providers they choose to establish a relationship of mutual trust
Keep in touch with the client during delivery, and help them resolve problems with the provider
Review with the client whether the provider delivered what was agreed, and use what you learn to improve future brokering

knowledgeRequirements.text: How to write a good brief for providers
Where to find specialist providers, and how to build and keep up to date a network of providers you can recommend impartially
How to compare providers' offers on cost, quality and fit
The meaning of common quality standards and accreditations held by providers
Procurement rules and the requirements for impartiality and independence where public funding is involved
How publicly funded support for specialist services usually works, including eligibility, client contributions and the conditions attached
The terms usually agreed for consultancy and other professional services to small businesses, and when to refer for legal advice
How to monitor and evaluate the work of a provider, and how to handle disputes
The records to keep of brokered support

standards.title: Working with Neurodivergent Clients
standards.whoFor: business advisers, mentors, coaches, trainers and other business support professionals who work with neurodivergent people who are starting or running businesses, and with businesses that employ or work with neurodivergent people.
standards.evolvedFrom: new Standard. Builds on Business and Enterprise Support (2013) unit 9 (knowledge items 8 and 13, the effects of disability on the client moving from opportunity to action, and the application of learning styles) and unit 20 (knowledge item 17, the learning styles shown by the client). The professional behaviours (B3 and B10) and the Core Standards (C1.K3, C3.K7 and C7.5) set out the inclusive practice every practitioner shows, and S4 covers adapting mentoring; S26 covers working with neurodivergent clients in depth. S27 covers working with disabled clients, and S24 covers reaching groups that are under-represented in business support.
standards.summary: This is about adapting your practice to how each neurodivergent client thinks, communicates and works, building on their strengths, and helping them shape their business around how they work best. It does not involve diagnosing anyone.

performanceRequirements.text: Ask every client how they prefer to communicate, take in information and work, without expecting them to disclose a diagnosis or condition, and act on what they tell you

Adapt how you deliver support and share information, for example by sending agendas and questions in advance, confirming what was agreed in writing, offering shorter or more frequent sessions, giving the client time to process and respond, and using plain language, visual summaries or recordings made with the client's consent
Agree meeting arrangements that suit the client, including the channel, place, time of day and sensory environment (for example lighting, noise and whether cameras are on in online meetings)

Keep anything the client tells you about being neurodivergent confidential, record it only with their agreement and only where it helps you support them, and handle it in line with data protection requirements

Help the client identify their strengths, interests and ways of working, and how these can give the business an advantage, without assuming that a particular diagnosis brings particular strengths or limits
Help the client shape their business model, role and working patterns around how they work best, including deciding what to do themselves and what to delegate, outsource or automate

Help the client set up practical systems for planning, prioritising, deadlines, money and record-keeping (for example reminders, templates, routines, and assistive and AI tools), and adjust them until they work
Help the client prepare for situations they find harder, such as networking, pitching, negotiating or handling complaints, and find approaches and support that suit them

Recognise signs that the client may be overloaded, close to burnout or under strain from hiding their differences (often called masking), talk about it with care, and help them adjust their workload and pace
Help the client decide whether, when and how to tell others, such as customers, funders, partners or staff, that they are neurodivergent, leaving the decision with them
Help the client find and apply for funded workplace support and assistive technology they may be eligible for, including as a self-employed person

Direct the client to assessment services, health professionals, mental health support or specialist organisations, or connect them with peer networks, role models and mentors (including other neurodivergent business owners), as they need and wish
Help clients who employ or work with neurodivergent people to understand good practice in recruitment, communication and reasonable adjustments, and refer them to HR or legal advice where needed

Seek feedback from neurodivergent clients on how well your support works for them, and raise with your organisation the parts of its processes, forms, eligibility rules, materials and venues that create barriers, suggesting changes

knowledgeRequirements.text: What neurodiversity and neurodivergence mean; the main forms of neurodivergence (for example autism, ADHD, dyslexia, dyspraxia, dyscalculia and Tourette's syndrome), how often they occur together and how much individuals vary; and the difference between specific learning differences, such as dyslexia, and learning disability

Respectful language: the different preferences people have (for example identity-first language such as "autistic person" and person-first language such as "person with ADHD"), why to follow each person's own preference, and terms to avoid, such as functioning labels and language that presents neurodivergence as suffering or as a superpower
The social model of disability, and how the design of services, systems and environments can create barriers for neurodivergent people
Executive function (for example planning, organising, prioritising, starting tasks, working memory and managing time), how it affects running a business, and practical strategies and tools that help
Differences in communication, social interaction, sensory processing and information processing, and how to adapt support for them

The strengths often associated with neurodivergence, the evidence on neurodivergent people in self-employment and business ownership and its limits, and why generalisations about any group can mislead
Masking, overload and burnout, how they can show, how they relate to mental health, and when to refer
Routes to assessment and diagnosis, waiting times, and why many neurodivergent people are undiagnosed or self-identify

Equality legislation as it applies to neurodivergent people, including when a person may meet the legal definition of disability, the duty of service providers to make reasonable adjustments (including anticipating the needs of disabled people), and the duties of employers
The data protection requirements for information about a person's health or disability, including the extra protection for special category data
Funded workplace support and assistive technology for neurodivergent people in work and self-employment, specialist organisations and peer networks, and how to keep up to date with changes to schemes
Good practice for employers in recruiting, managing and supporting neurodivergent staff, at an awareness level, and when to refer

standards.title: Working with Disabled Clients
standards.whoFor: business advisers, mentors, coaches, trainers and other business support professionals who work with disabled people, including people with long-term or fluctuating health conditions, who are starting or running businesses, and with businesses that employ disabled people or serve disabled customers.
standards.evolvedFrom: new Standard. Builds on Business and Enterprise Support (2013) unit 9 (knowledge item 8, the effects of disability on the client moving from opportunity to action) and unit 5 (knowledge item 26, the business benefits of engaging with equality and diversity), and on the behaviour common to many 2013 units of recognising the opportunities presented by the diversity of people. The professional behaviours (B3 and B10) and the Core Standards (C1.K2, C1.K3, C3.K7 and C7.5) set out the inclusive practice every practitioner shows; S27 covers working with disabled clients in depth. S26 covers working with neurodivergent clients, and S24 covers reaching groups that are under-represented in business support.
standards.summary: This is about removing the barriers that support itself can create for disabled clients, making your support accessible, and helping clients build businesses that fit their lives and reach disabled customers. It does not involve giving clinical or welfare benefits advice.

performanceRequirements.text: Ask every client what would help them take part fully in the support, without expecting them to disclose an impairment or condition, and act on what they tell you

Make meetings, events and online sessions accessible (for example step-free venues, accessible toilets and parking, hearing loops, live captions and accessible online platforms), and check arrangements with the client in advance
Provide information in formats the client can use, such as large print, Easy Read, audio, or digital documents that work with screen readers and other assistive technology

Book British Sign Language interpreters, other communication professionals and support workers in good time where they are needed, agree roles with them in advance, and speak directly to the client rather than to the person supporting them
Plan support around fluctuating and long-term conditions, including flexible timing, the option to rearrange without penalty, and a pace that suits the client's energy

Keep anything the client tells you about an impairment or health condition confidential, record it only with their agreement and only where it helps you support them, and handle it in line with data protection requirements
Help the client design a business and working pattern that fit their circumstances, including hours, place of work, pace, and what to delegate, outsource or automate
Help the client understand, at an awareness level, how starting or running a business may affect any disability benefits they receive, and refer them to specialist welfare benefits advice

Help the client find and apply for funded workplace support, equipment, adaptations and assistive technology, including what is available to self-employed people, and plan for the time applications can take
Help the client make their products, services, premises and online presence accessible to disabled customers, and see the market opportunity in doing so
Help the client decide whether, when and how to tell others, such as customers, funders, partners or staff, about an impairment or condition, leaving the decision with them
Connect the client with disabled people's organisations, specialist charities, peer networks, role models and mentors, where they would value this
Help clients who employ, or want to employ, disabled people to understand good practice in recruitment, reasonable adjustments and funded support, and refer them to HR or legal advice where needed

Seek feedback from disabled clients on how accessible your support is, and raise with your organisation the parts of its venues, platforms, materials, processes and eligibility rules that create barriers, suggesting changes

knowledgeRequirements.text: The social model of disability and how it differs from the medical model, and how barriers in services, environments, information, attitudes and systems disable people

Respectful language, including "disabled people" and "non-disabled people", the terms d/Deaf, British Sign Language user, hard of hearing, blind and sight loss, terms to avoid (for example "the disabled", "handicapped", "wheelchair-bound" and "suffers from"), and why to follow each person's own preference

The range of impairments and conditions (physical, sensory, mental health, learning disability, and long-term and fluctuating conditions), how many are not visible, and why not to make assumptions from a label

Equality legislation as it applies across the UK nations, including the legal definition of disability, the duty of service providers to make reasonable adjustments (including anticipating the needs of disabled people), the duties of employers, and the legal recognition of British Sign Language
Accessibility good practice and standards for venues, events, documents, digital content and online meetings
How to work with British Sign Language interpreters, other communication professionals, personal assistants and support workers
How fluctuating and long-term conditions, pain and fatigue can affect running a business, and how to plan for them
How self-employment can interact with disability benefits, at an awareness level, and where to find specialist welfare benefits advice
Funded workplace support, equipment, adaptations and assistive technology for disabled people in work and self-employment, and how to keep up to date with changes to schemes
The data protection requirements for information about a person's health or disability, including the extra protection for special category data
Disabled customers as a market, and the principles of inclusive design for products, services, premises and online presence
Disabled people's organisations, specialist charities and peer networks; good practice for employers in recruiting and supporting disabled staff, at an awareness level; and when to refer

standards.title: Respond to enquiries and identify needs
standards.evolvedFrom: Business Information 1 (Deal with initial business information enquiries from clients and identify their needs).
standards.summary: This is about responding to enquiries from people who are starting or running businesses, whether by phone, email, web chat, social media or in person. It involves asking the right questions to find out what they really need, providing information or directing them to the right support, and building their confidence in the service.

performanceRequirements.text: Deal with enquiries promptly, politely and in line with your service's standards, whatever the channel
Encourage the client to explain what they need, and ask questions that uncover their real needs beyond the initial enquiry
Ask for advice and guidance when you are not confident that you understand the client's business needs
Manage the client's expectations about what the service can provide, including the benefits, limitations, timescales and any costs
Provide information, or direct the client to specialist information, advice or support, giving contact details or making introductions where appropriate
Explain the scope of your organisation's services and any funded support the client may be eligible for
Check that the client has understood the information, pacing it to suit them
Keep accurate and secure records of each enquiry and the action taken, in line with data protection requirements
Assure the client that their information is confidential, and explain how it will be used and when it will be shared with their consent
Close each contact in a way that makes the client want to come back

knowledgeRequirements.text: Interpersonal and communication skills for handling enquiries, including listening, questioning, reflecting back, checking accuracy, summarising and dealing with difficulties
The benefits and drawbacks of different channels (for example phone, email, web chat, social media, video and face to face), and how to handle enquiries well in each
How to communicate with people whose first language is not English and with people who have different communication needs
How people take in information differently, and how to pace and present it so that it can be understood
How to recognise the nature of an enquiry and why the client needs the information
How business needs vary by size, stage of development, sector and type (private, social enterprise and voluntary)
The answers to frequently asked questions
The services your organisation provides, and the local and national support you can direct clients to, including eligibility and referral routes
How to triage enquiries and decide when and where to refer
The limits of your own role, skills and knowledge, and when and where to get advice
The data protection rules that apply to enquiries and client records

standards.title: Find and provide business information
standards.evolvedFrom: Business Information 2 (Research and provide clients with the business information they need).
standards.summary: This is about researching and providing business information that is accurate, reliable and relevant to the client. It involves identifying and judging sources, collecting and analysing information, and presenting it clearly. It includes using online research and AI tools, and checking what they produce.

performanceRequirements.text: Establish exactly what information the client needs, and how much
Find possible sources of information and judge each for reliability, currency and relevance, giving priority to authoritative sources
Search for and collect information efficiently, using appropriate methods and tools, including online databases and search
Use AI and other digital tools to help find and summarise information where appropriate, and check the results against reliable sources
Analyse and interpret the information accurately and draw suitable conclusions
Identify gaps, conflicting information or unexpected results, and deal with them
Present the information clearly, in a form that suits the client and their needs
Acknowledge sources, and respect copyright and licensing terms
Protect confidential information, and comply with relevant legislation, codes of practice and ethical requirements
Record the information provided and the sources used

knowledgeRequirements.text: The main sources of business information and their strengths and weaknesses, including official statistics, government and regulatory guidance, market research, company information, local information, business directories and specialist publications

Where to find authoritative information on the legislation and regulation affecting businesses (for example employment, health and safety, tax, environmental protection, intellectual property, data protection and international trade)
Search techniques, and how to use online databases and information systems effectively
How to judge the quality, currency and reliability of information, including online and AI-generated content
How to analyse and summarise information, including simple data
How to present different types of business information clearly for different audiences
Copyright, licensing and how to acknowledge sources
The confidentiality and data protection requirements that apply to research

standards.title: Administer and promote business information and support services
standards.evolvedFrom: Business Information 3 (Contribute to administering and promoting business information services).
standards.summary: This is about the day-to-day administration that enables an effective information and support service, including client records, diaries and bookings, and the events and communications that promote the service. It applies to services delivered in person, online or both.

performanceRequirements.text: Set up and update client records in line with legal requirements and organisational guidelines, using your organisation's client relationship management system
Maintain complete, accurate and up-to-date records of client contacts and follow-up
Plan and manage your own and colleagues' diaries and bookings to meet deadlines
Prepare and supply information that tells clients and others about the services available, in print and online
Plan and organise meetings, events and webinars that promote and provide business support
Present the service in a way that clearly explains its benefits to different audiences
Monitor customer satisfaction and contribute to improving the service

knowledgeRequirements.text: What should be recorded about client contacts and follow-up, and how to use your organisation's client relationship management system
The data protection and confidentiality requirements that apply to client records
How to prioritise and balance competing demands, and how to manage diaries and bookings
How to plan in-person and online events, including resources, accessibility, health and safety, invitations and follow-up
How to promote services through different channels, including websites, email and social media
Customer service standards, and how to measure and improve customer satisfaction
The common problems customers experience and how to solve them

standards.title: Provide and maintain information resources
standards.evolvedFrom: Business Information 4 (Provide and maintain the materials needed to deliver business information).
standards.summary: This is about keeping the information resources used by the service and its clients accurate, accessible and up to date. Resources may include web pages, guides, frequently asked questions, knowledge bases, templates and video, as well as printed materials.

performanceRequirements.text: Review the information resources used by the service and its clients, and how they are used
Consult users and colleagues on how well the resources meet their needs
Identify future needs, and trends in how people look for and use information
Obtain or create resources that meet identified needs, within the resources available
Organise and store resources so that people can easily find what they need
Keep resources accurate and up to date, and remove or correct out-of-date information
Make sure resources are accessible, including for disabled people
Protect resources from damage, inappropriate use or alteration
Evaluate the effectiveness of resources, and recommend improvements with a clear rationale and supporting evidence
Make sure resources comply with legislation, codes of practice and copyright

knowledgeRequirements.text: The types and formats of information resources used by business support services
How to find out how resources are used and what users need
How information technologies, including search and AI tools, are changing the way people find and use information
How to structure, index and organise information so that it can be found easily
How often resources should be reviewed, and how to keep information current
Accessibility standards for digital content
Copyright and licensing for information resources
How to evaluate the effectiveness of resources and make the case for improvements

standards.title: Build relationships with others
standards.evolvedFrom: Introduction to Enterprise Support 1 (Build relationships with others); Business and Enterprise Support (2013) unit 3.
standards.summary: This is about building rapport with people, helping them develop trust and confidence in you, and reviewing how your relationship with them is going. It involves communicating effectively, in person and remotely, so that you can find out what you need to know, listening, reflecting and getting your point across clearly.

performanceRequirements.text: Find out about the people you work with, including what motivates them and what they want to achieve
Adjust how you work to suit the people you are working with
Choose the right way to talk and share information, whether in person, by phone, by video or in writing
Give people your full attention when they are speaking
Play back what you have heard to check you have understood it correctly
Get your point across in a way the other person can follow
Question answers constructively when something does not add up, and clear up misunderstandings
Notice when someone seems worried about something, and raise it gently
Keep in touch with each person in the ways that suit them
Check with the people you work with how the relationship is working for them

knowledgeRequirements.text: Why it helps to get to know the people you work with (for example to build trust and to tailor your help)
What drives the people you work with, and the pressures and responsibilities they carry
That people differ in how they prefer to work and communicate, including people with different communication needs
How to go into conversations with an open mind, without deciding the outcome in advance
Basic communication skills: listening, asking questions, summarising, playing back what you have heard, constructive challenge, negotiating, feedback and handling difficulties
The spoken and unspoken signs that someone is worried or concerned
When different ways of communicating work well, and when they do not
When and how to check how a relationship is going

standards.title: Use your expertise and experience to help others
standards.evolvedFrom: Introduction to Enterprise Support 2 (Use your expertise and experience to help others); Business and Enterprise Support (2013) unit 6.
standards.summary: This is about helping others to benefit from your expertise and experience. It involves clarifying what people need, explaining issues and ideas clearly, and recognising the limits of your own expertise and knowledge.

performanceRequirements.text: Help the person you are working with to say clearly what they want to achieve
Work out what is expected of you, and be clear about what you can and cannot offer
Use what you have learned and experienced in the ways that will help them most
Explain things you are expert in using terms the other person can follow and use
Notice whether things are going well or not, and act on it
Spot when someone needs help beyond your expertise, and help them find it elsewhere

knowledgeRequirements.text: How to agree at the start what each of you hopes to get from the relationship
Where your role begins and ends
Which parts of your experience make your help more relevant and credible
What you do not know, and the limits of your skills and experience
The signs that someone needs personal support or specialist professional advice
Where else people can get help, and when to point them there
How to keep information about the people you work with confidential and secure

standards.title: Evaluate and develop your own performance
standards.evolvedFrom: Introduction to Enterprise Support 3 (Evaluate and develop your own performance); Business and Enterprise Support (2013) units 17 and 18 (in part).
standards.summary: This is about reflecting honestly on your own performance and finding ways to improve it. It involves working with others to identify your strengths and weaknesses, finding out what information and support is available, and developing and following a plan that covers your personal and professional aspirations.

performanceRequirements.text: Keep an eye on how well you are doing, and look for ways to do better
Ask the people you work with for feedback, regularly
Work out what you need to improve and which skills to develop, on your own or with others' help
Keep your knowledge current enough to do your role well
Act on feedback, and try new approaches
Keep a personal development plan, and update it as your aims change and you achieve them

knowledgeRequirements.text: What you value and want from your career and life, and how this connects to your role
Why reviewing your own performance and building your skills matters
Simple ways to review your own performance, and who can give you useful feedback
What goes into a development plan, and how to keep it up to date
The knowledge, understanding and skills your role requires
The sources of information, learning and support that can help you develop, including online learning

standards.title: Help others to set and realise objectives
standards.evolvedFrom: Introduction to Enterprise Support 4 (Help others to set and realise objectives); Business and Enterprise Support (2013) unit 8.
standards.summary: This is about developing a clear picture of what the person you are working with wants to achieve, and helping them achieve it. It includes setting objectives, identifying risks and how to manage them, working out what resources are needed, and finding others who can help.

performanceRequirements.text: Help the person you are working with to set objectives they can realistically achieve
Help them sort what is essential from what would be nice to have, and prioritise
Agree a plan with them that leaves room for them to shape it
Spot what might get in the way
Weigh up the options with them, looking at strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, threats, risks and benefits
Work out what resources they will need and how to get them
Bring in others who can help, and help the person get any further support they need

knowledgeRequirements.text: What the person wants to achieve and what it will take (for example resources, other people's commitment, skills, knowledge and information)
How to set clear, measurable objectives with timescales
How to spot and size up the obstacles to progress
Simple risk assessment and planning techniques
How to handle the changes that achieving the objectives may bring
When a need goes beyond what you know, and where to find other support

standards.title: Understand how small businesses work
standards.evolvedFrom: Introduction to Enterprise Support 5 (Knowledge and experience of a small business and its core functions); Business Information 8; Business and Enterprise Support (2013) unit 7 (in part).
standards.summary: If you want to work in business support, you need knowledge or experience of the essential areas of business, including finance, marketing, sales and customer service, and how they link to and support each other. You also need an understanding of the demands, pressures and motivations facing the people who run businesses. This Standard sets that knowledge at an introductory level, as a basis for progressing to the Core Standards (C6 sets the level expected of a business support professional).

performanceRequirements.text: Apply a basic understanding of how a small business works when helping others
Recognise how the main functions of a business link to and affect each other
Show an understanding of the pressures and motivations of the people who run businesses

knowledgeRequirements.text: How to work out how much money a business needs, where it can come from and what funders look for
How money moves in and out of a business, and how to forecast and track it
Opening and managing a business bank account, and understanding basic financial accounts
Common accounting terms, and the basics of business tax and record-keeping
Market research, understanding what customers want, and knowing who the competition is
Basic marketing and sales techniques and tools, including websites, social media and selling online
What good customer service looks like and how to check it is being delivered, and the basics of terms of business
The legal forms a business can take, and the basic legal requirements of running one (for example registration, licences, insurance and data protection)
How digital tools, including AI, are used in running a small business
How much of themselves people put into their businesses, and the time and energy it takes
The main parts of a small business and how they depend on each other
What starting and running a small business well involves, and the pressures that pull owners in different directions
The range of abilities business owners need, and the risks they take on

whatsNew: AI and Digital Adoption (S3), Supporting Businesses in Difficulty (S11), Rural and Land-based Business (S15), Creative Industries (S16) and Business Resilience (S17) are new Specialist Standards
Business Model and Value Proposition Design (S19) is a new Specialist Standard on using visual tools such as canvases to design, test and improve how a business creates and earns from value
Developing Enterprising Skills (S18) brings forward the 2013 standard on enterprising skills, for people on any path, not only those starting a business

Brokering Specialist Support (S25) brings together the original standards on assessing and brokering providers' offers, so that C4 can focus on the finding, explaining and referring every practitioner does

Consultative Advisory Practice (S20), Action Learning Facilitation (S21), Business Account Management (S22), Digital Marketing and Social Media (S23) and Inclusive Engagement with Under-represented Businesses (S24) are new Specialist Standards that give depth to the advisory, facilitation, relationship and outreach skills set out in the Core Standards

Working with Neurodivergent Clients (S26) and Working with Disabled Clients (S27) are new Specialist Standards that develop the 2013 standards' attention to disability, diversity and learning styles into full Standards on making support accessible and adapting it to how each client thinks, communicates and works
Ethical and professional practice (C7) is now a Standard in its own right, rather than being left to the guidelines of each organisation
Reaching and engaging potential clients is now part of the Core Standards (C1)
The Business Information and Introduction suites keep their original numbering (I1 to I4 and E1 to E5), updated for digital channels, online research and AI, accessibility and data protection
Measuring and evidencing impact (C5) is drawn together into a single Standard
Data protection, digital and remote delivery, and the responsible use of AI are built into the Core Standards
Mentoring and coaching, previously treated as modes of consulting, now have their own Specialist Standards (S4 and S5)
The personal behaviours repeated in every original unit are set out once (B1 to B11)
Dated references (for example to Business Link, regional economic strategies, fax and named funding schemes) have been removed, and duplicated units have been merged
